key_terms: The store, JanusGraph in Atlas, that persists entities and relationships, commonly on HBase. Its durability decides what survives a restart.
The index backend, such as Solr, that serves Atlas discovery queries. It can lag or be unavailable while graph reads succeed.
Entities and lineage that remain readable by GUID after Atlas and its backing services restart, which holds only if the graph storage itself survived.
Whether graph and index backups capture the same point in time, so a restore does not leave search out of step with stored entities.
The set of components that fail together. Containers on one Docker engine share one host, so restarting them cannot prove disaster recovery.

worked_examples.title: Record identities, restart, then check only
worked_examples.code:
cd work/atlas
bash run.sh check
bash run.sh check
worked_examples.interpretation: Run check once before the server lifecycle change and once after, without apply in between. Both receipts should list identical entity_guids and both expected edges. Because check is read-only, any difference points at persistence: the graph store in HBase or Cassandra lost writes, or the server came back attached to a different backend. Running apply to fix a gap would recreate entities with new GUIDs and destroy the evidence.

worked_examples.title: Graph read versus index search after recovery
worked_examples.interpretation: The first call reads from the graph store; the second goes through the Solr or Elasticsearch index. If the GUID read succeeds while search returns fewer entities, the data survived and the index is behind or needs a rebuild. If both fail, the graph is the problem. Keeping the two observations separate prevents a full restore when a reindex would have been enough.

evidence: Complete real Atlas REST payload/client route with default local server omitted. Native compatible server preparation and actual API/graph/index/lifecycle acceptance are explicit separate work, never simulated execution.
